analysis.one_liner: Bars federal emergency orders from keeping fossil fuel plants running at ratepayers' expense.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2026 with 4 Democratic cosponsors, the bill has sat in the Senate Energy Committee since its first day with no hearing, no vote, and no action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would restrict an emergency power in the Federal Power Act (Section 202(c)) that lets federal officials order power plants to stay online during grid emergencies. It would bar orders that block a fossil fuel plant's retirement unless there is truly no other way to meet the emergency and the regional grid operator asks for it in writing. It would also require a public hearing, a public online docket, an analysis of alternatives, estimates of added costs, and written notice to utility customers about what an emergency order is adding to their bills.
analysis.who_benefits: Electricity customers, who currently absorb the costs of keeping uneconomic fossil plants running — extra fuel, maintenance, capital, and labor — through their power bills when the government issues an emergency order. Utilities that have planned to retire plants would be freer to close them, and communities dealing with pollution from plants kept alive past their planned shutdown would see them retire sooner. [S2]

how_it_helps.text: Blocks the most common use of emergency orders against ratepayers: the bill adds a rule that federal regulators may not issue an order preventing or delaying a power plant's permanent retirement, unless an emergency truly cannot be met any other way and the regional transmission organization requests the delay in writing.

Puts costs on the record before they land on bills: any emergency order must be published on a public docket and accompanied by a report analyzing the cause of the emergency, alternatives considered, and estimated additional system costs — including extra fuel, maintenance, capital, and labor — expected to fall on utilities and their customers.

Requires utilities to tell customers directly: within 60 days of an emergency order, each affected electric utility must send written notice describing the order and its cost impacts, with a link to the order.

Adds process and accountability: before issuing an order, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission would have to hold a public hearing, determine whether the order will raise rates for ratepayers and conflict with environmental laws, consult state and local regulators, and consider alternatives that meet the emergency with minimal environmental harm. Repeated orders about the same facility would count as renewals and trigger the full set of requirements each time.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of fossil fuel plants would lose the revenue that comes from emergency orders requiring plants to stay online after they were slated to retire — costs that today are passed to ratepayers. Coal-dependent towns and plant workers could face earlier shutdowns. In a genuine grid crisis, if alternatives fall short, all customers could face reliability risk; the bill keeps only a narrow carve-out where no alternative exists and the grid operator asks for the delay. [S2]
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil plant owners; possibly grid reliability

drawbacks.text: Reliability risk in a real crisis: the bill removes 'other causes' from the emergency definition and requires a public hearing, ratepayer and environmental analysis, and state consultation before renewing an order, and it lets a plant's retirement proceed unless there is no alternative and the grid operator requests a delay in writing — which could slow or prevent a forced run in a genuine emergency.

Earlier plant retirements fall hardest on coal-dependent communities: the bill's core prohibition is on orders that delay a plant's permanent closure, which would speed shutdowns in towns where a plant is the main employer and tax base.

Slower response in the window that matters: for initial orders the analysis and cost-estimate requirements apply only 'to the maximum extent practicable,' but for any renewed or reissued order the commission must fully comply — meaning a plant kept online through a long emergency faces repeated hearings and consultations while it runs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For electricity customers, the benefit is straightforward: today, emergency orders can force a plant slated for retirement to keep burning fuel, with the bill passed to ratepayers and no notice of who is paying. The bill stops that in most cases and forces costs into public view. The cost is a small risk to grid reliability in genuine emergencies, softened by a narrow carve-out where no alternative exists and the grid operator asks for the delay. The design is lopsided in consumers' favor by intent; the main honest objection is that a future crisis is exactly when process requirements hurt most.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee the same day, and it has had no hearing, markup, or vote since.

narrative.text: Senator Ed Markey introduced the bill on April 16, 2026, joined by four Democratic colleagues — Senators Welch, Van Hollen, Merkley, and Blunt Rochester.

The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, which is the standard first step; no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled since.

The bill would rewrite Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act, the emergency authority the federal government has used to order plants to keep running; in its current form, such orders can be issued without notice, hearing, or report, and the bill strikes that language.
The 119th Congress runs until January 3, 2027, so the bill is technically alive, but with Republicans holding 55 Senate seats and no Republican support, it remains parked in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, the status quo: owners of fossil fuel plants continue to receive revenue from emergency orders that keep them running, while the ratepayers who fund those costs get no such bill, hearing, or vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, fossil plant owners; bill still pending

for.name: Ed Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to limit Federal Power Act emergency orders that keep fossil plants online at ratepayers' expense.

for.name: 4 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Senators Welch, Van Hollen, Merkley, and Blunt Rochester)

against.name: John Barrasso (or current Energy chair)
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and has scheduled no hearing, markup, or vote; the bill has not moved since its introduction day.

against.name: Fossil fuel power plant owners
against.what_they_did: Have collected revenue under emergency orders requiring plants slated for retirement to keep running, with costs passed to ratepayers — the practice the bill would end; no organized public opposition to the bill itself is on the record.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or public opposition yet: all five sponsors are Democrats (4 of 45 Senate Democrats plus Markey), no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-run committee has simply not acted.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel power plant owners (coal and gas)
industries.note: The bill cuts off the main revenue channel these plants get from federal emergency orders requiring them to run after their planned retirement — a cost today billed to electricity customers. Their interest in keeping the current authority runs directly against the ratepayers who pay for it.

The bill requires regulators, to the maximum extent practicable, to consider alternatives that meet an emergency with minimal environmental impact, and it lets planned plant retirements proceed — shifting future grid investment away from keeping old fossil units alive.
The bill gives them a formal gatekeeping role — a written request is required to delay any retirement — while leaving them exposed if reliability falters under tighter limits on emergency orders.

analysis.trajectory: With a 55-seat Republican Senate majority, no Republican cosponsors, and no committee action in the months since referral, the likely path is the usual one for a minority-party energy bill: no hearing or markup, and the bill dies in committee when the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
